title: 2.2 Small Group · Group 2
contentObjective: I can go beyond today's lesson: divide a whole number by a fraction by multiplying by the reciprocal in trickier cases, and explain WHY it works.
languageObjective: I can justify my answer to a skeptic and connect it to a second strategy or representation.

revealWordProblem.title: Apply: Evidence Bags
revealWordProblem.text: Agent Park has 6 pounds of evidence powder to log. Each labeled evidence bag holds exactly 2/3 of a pound. How many bags can Agent Park fill with all 6 pounds? Explain your reasoning.

turnAndTalk.question: Agent Park has 4 pounds of evidence powder and fills bags that hold 1/2 pound each. How many bags can he fill, and how do you know?
turnAndTalk.kernel: Each whole pound makes 2 half-pound bags, so 4 pounds makes 8 bags.

turnAndTalk.listenFor: Students see that 4 ÷ 1/2 = 8 and explain there are 2 halves in each whole pound.

turnAndTalk.question: How does 'Keep, Change, Flip' turn 6 ÷ 1/3 into a multiplication problem?
turnAndTalk.kernel: I keep the 6, change ÷ to ×, and flip 1/3 to its reciprocal 3.

turnAndTalk.question: When would dividing a whole number by a fraction help you in real life?
turnAndTalk.kernel: It tells you how many fraction-size portions fit into a whole amount.

conceptIntro.heading: Push further — How do I divide a whole number by a fraction?
conceptIntro.intro: You already can do this. In this group we go deeper: trickier numbers, a second way to see it, and explaining why it works — not just getting the answer.
conceptIntro.keyIdea: Dividing by a fraction is the same as multiplying by its reciprocal (the fraction flipped over). — and you can explain WHY, and predict when it gets tricky.

iDo.title: Watch me
lines: Agent Park has 4 pounds of powder and each bag holds 1/2 pound. I want 4 ÷ 1/2.
Keep the 4. Change ÷ to ×. Flip 1/2 to make 2/1, which is just 2.
So 4 ÷ 1/2 = 8. He can fill 8 bags. That makes sense: each pound fills 2 bags, and 4 pounds × 2 = 8.

weDo.title: Generalize it
lines: Start from what you know: Let's try 3 ÷ 1/4 together. What do we keep? The 3.
Now predict: what happens with much bigger numbers, or numbers that share no common factors? Make a prediction, then check it.

youDo.title: Take the challenge
lines: Work the challenge problems below. For each one, be ready to justify your answer to a skeptic.
If you finish early: find a second strategy, or a case where it would break.

explore.instructions: Go deeper: Use the number line to show how many 1/2-size jumps fit into 4. As you work, ask yourself WHY it works.
explore.label: Show 4 ÷ 1/2 on the number line
explore.questionText: How many jumps of 1/2 does it take to get from 0 to 4?

discourse.prompt: Why does 4 ÷ 1/2 = 8? How does the number line show this?
discourse.sentenceFrame: 4 ÷ 1/2 = 8 because it takes ___ jumps of ___ to get from 0 to ___.

choiceFeedback: That's multiplication. Are we finding groups or finding how many pieces fit?
Division by a fraction asks 'how many fit,' not multiplication.
That's computing division by whole numbers. Remember: dividing by 1/3 is different.
hints: The divisor is 2/3 — not a unit fraction — so the flip matters even more here.
Keep 6, change ÷ to ×, and flip the whole fraction 2/3 (both numbers trade places).
2/3 flips to 3/2, giving 6 × 3/2. Multiply, then simplify the result before choosing.

onLevel.title: onLevel — Spot the Common Mistake

workedExample.label: Keep, Change, Flip
workedExample.work: Flipped the wrong number — wrote 1/8 × 3/4 instead of 8 × 4/3

onLevel.correctWork: Keep the dividend 8 the same and flip only the divisor: 8 × 4/3 = 32/3 = 10 2/3. The mistake was flipping the whole number 8 into 1/8 instead of flipping the divisor 3/4 into 4/3.
hints: Only the divisor (the fraction you are dividing by) gets flipped — the 8 stays as 8.

extending.title: Find the Division Error
extending.correctWork: 6 × 3/2 (flip the divisor 2/3 to get 3/2, not keep it as 2/3). Then 6 × 3/2 = 18/2 = 9.
hints: In 'Keep, Change, Flip' — which fraction gets flipped?
The divisor (2/3) should become its reciprocal (3/2). Did Step 2 flip the right fraction?

extending.prompt: A pizza shop has 8 whole pizzas. Each serving is 2/3 of a pizza. How many servings can they make? Write and solve an equation, then explain why the answer is greater than 8.
extending.sentenceFrame: The equation is 8 ÷ 2/3 = ___. Using Keep, Change, Flip: 8 × 3/2 = ___. The answer is greater than 8 because ___.
extending.hint: Compare dividing by 2 (whole) vs dividing by 1/2 (fraction). Why is one answer bigger?
hints: Re-read: 8 whole pizzas, and each serving takes 2/3 of one pizza — servings are smaller than a pizza.
Set up total ÷ serving size, use Keep, Change, Flip, then explain why the count beats 8.
Flip 2/3 to 3/2 and set up 8 × 3/2. Finish it, then explain: each pizza serves more than one person, so…

extending.label: Compare: what happens when you divide the same whole number by different fractions?
extending.hint: Look for the pattern: as denominators change, how does the quotient change?
hints: The dividend 12 never changes — only the divisor does. Track what the quotient does row by row.
Flip each divisor and multiply. Then compare: does a bigger divisor give more pieces or fewer?
Row one: 12 ÷ 1/2 → 12 × 2. Compute it, then check whether the next row's quotient goes up or down.

practice.commonMistake: A common mistake in Divide Whole Numbers by Fractions is doing 'Keep, Change' but skipping the 'Flip' — students multiply by the divisor as it is instead of by its reciprocal. For example, for 6 ÷ 3/4, a student might write 6 × 3/4 = 4 1/2 and stop there, but the divisor 3/4 must be flipped to 4/3 first: 6 × 4/3 = 24/3 = 8. Before you submit, check: did I flip the second fraction (the divisor) upside down before multiplying?

diagram.caption: One foot of rope splits into four 1/4-foot markers, so each whole foot makes 4 markers and all 10 feet make 10 x 4 = 40 (10 divided by 1/4 = 40).

connect.promptQuestion: How does dividing a whole number by a fraction help the detective?
connect.prompt: The detective can set up ___ markers because 10 ÷ 1/4 = ___.

hints: 9 ÷ 1/3 asks how many 1/3-size pieces fit into 9 wholes — predict more or fewer than 9 first.
Keep, Change, Flip: keep the 9, change ÷ to ×, and flip 1/3 before multiplying.

smallGroup.label: Challenge
smallGroup.who: Pull students who showed mastery on the formative check and are ready to extend.
moves: Launch the challenge fast — skip the re-teach, they don't need it.
Step back. Let them wrestle; protect the productive struggle.
Ask "How do you know?" and "Can you show it a second way?" more than you explain.
Push for a generalization: when does this hold, and when would it break?
Close by having one student justify a claim to the group.
